7559.t: Unknown. Ionic word for "lizard" (common being σαύρα (saúra)), perhaps from κρόκη (krókē, “pebble”) + δρῖλος (drîlos, “worm”), because crocodiles like resting on flat stones.

7564.t: A Semitic loanword. Compare Akkadian 𒌑𒆪𒄀𒆸𒈾 (/⁠kurkanū⁠/), Arabic كُرْكُم (kurkum), and Hebrew כרכום (karkom).

7586.t: Uncertain. Sometimes considered a Pre-Greek substrate word.

7592.t: A vinicultural loan of Semitic origin, compare Hebrew כַּד (kad), Ugaritic 𐎋𐎄 (kd), Imperial Aramaic 𐡊𐡃 (kd), Punic 𐤊𐤃 (kd).

7582.t: Not related to κύπη (kúpē, “kind of ship”), nor derived from κύπτω (kúptō, “to bend, stoop”). According to Beekes, clearly a Pre-Greek word, given the variant.

7533.t: Traditionally derived from κνίζω (knízō, “scratch or gash”); yet the -ι- is long in this word, which may point to Pre-Greek origin, according to Beekes.

7570.t: Reminiscent of δοῦπος (doûpos, “thud”), but further details are unknown. The variation between voiced and unvoiced stop suggests Pre-Greek origin.

7598.t: From the stem of κατόψομαι (katópsomai) (root *h₃ekʷ- (“to see”)), future of καθοράω (kathoráō, “to behold”) + -τρον (-tron, instrument suffix).

7588.t: Probably from a Mediterranean Pre-Greek substrate word, as hinted by the suffixes. Traditionally linked to Proto-Indo-European *ḱer- (“head, top, skull, horn”).

7597.t: From κάρφω (kárphō, “to dry up, to wither”) + -ος (-os). Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐂓 (ka+po).

7547.t: Perhaps related to κόρυς (kórŭs, “helmet”), referring to the thick end of the weapon. According to Beekes, the word is of Pre-Greek origin.

7526.t: From the root of κλίνω (klī́nō, “to lie down; to recline”).

7505.t: The connection with καῖρος (kaîros, “string”) seems obvious. The presence of the alternative forms leads to a Pre-Greek origin.

7596.t: The word has been connected with Persian کبر (kabar, “caper”) and Burushaski [script needed] (čopuri) (a language isolate), suggesting an Oriental origin.

7522.t: According to Beekes, from Pre-Greek. Furnée compares κιθάρα (kĭthắrā, “ivy”).

7595.t: Uncertain. * The origin of the beetle-name is unclear, but it may be an r-stem-suffixation to κάνθων (kánthōn, “pack-ass”) as suggested by Strömberg, since the scarab is recognized for and likened by his transporting packs of dung.

7566.t: From κεράννυμι (keránnumi, “to mix”) and the suffix -μα (-ma).

7565.t: A similar word for "onion" and "garlic" is found in Proto-West Germanic *hramusō (“onion, garlic”), Proto-Slavic *čermъša (“ramson”) and Middle Irish crem (“wild garlic”), suggesting a derivation from Proto-Indo-European *kermus- (“wild garlic”).

7572.t: Given the unusual formation, according to Beekes, the word is without a doubt Pre-Greek. Frisk and Chantraine discuss it under κυδάζω (kudázō, “to insult”), but the semantic relation seems weak.

7534.t: Based on the stem forms κνιδ-, κνισ- (knid-, knis-), likely from a Proto-Indo-European *kneyd- (“to scratch, knock”), from *ken- (“to scratch; scrape; rub”).

7546.t: An iterative deverbative verb, lacking a good etymology.
